references/bpc/population-general/mobility-built-environment.md:15:### Best-practice synthesis
references/bpc/population-general/mobility-built-environment.md:18:**Most targeted provision:** Differentiated specification across device type — manual wheelchair (1500 mm minimum / 1700 mm best practice), power wheelchair (1700–1800 mm), scooter and large power device (1800+ mm) — with OT-assessed co-design resolving the specific value at Tier 2. Habinteg Inclusive Housing Design Guide (2024, RCOTSS-Housing OT authored) is the highest-authority source for room-by-room residential turning space targets.
references/bpc/population-general/mobility-built-environment.md:22:**Highest-ambition actionable specification:** Turning space ≥1800 mm diameter for typical power-WC accommodation [Co-1/Tier 2 — IWA BPAG p.29; Tier 5 — BS 8300-2]; **2400 mm where IDEA + BS8300 entire-sample evidence applies (Steinfeld 2006, Tier 3)**, particularly for settings serving bariatric or large-power-WC users; 1925 mm acceptable where UDI sub-sample 180° methodology applies (open-ended bay; Steinfeld 2006); 1700 mm acceptable where space-constrained [Tier 5 — RHFAC CA]; 1700 mm minimum floor [Tier 5 — RHFAC CA / BS8300 UK]. Note: ADA 1524 mm rejected as a design baseline — cited here as evidence of regulatory lag only, not as a permitted specification value. Ramp gradient: 1:20 (5%) ideal [Tier 5]; 1:16 intermediate; 1:12 (8.3%) code minimum with rest platforms every 9 m [Tier 6]. Door clear opening: 900 mm best practice; 850 mm minimum for power WC (CSA B651). SIA 500:2009 (CH): ramp max 6%; admissible to 12% with handrails. NCC 2022/BCA 2024 (AU): AS 1428.1:2021 turning circle 1500 mm × 1500 mm (Tier 6); Summer Foundation/UTS research confirms AS 1428.1 under-accommodates power WC users — same pattern as US. BCA Code 2025 (SG, effective Nov 2025): now includes anthropometric data for power WC users; wheelchair manoeuvring space requirements updated. DL 163/2006 (PT): 1500 mm turning circle for manual WC only — explicitly acknowledged as insufficient for electric WC by authors. DM 236/89 (IT): accessibility/visitability/adaptability three-tier framework; turning space 1500 mm minimum, no power WC provision. 편의증진법 2024 (KR): major 2024 revision shifts from route access to daily life access; 1500 mm manoeuvre space for WC; noted as manual WC basis. NBR 9050:2020 (BR): 360° rotation = 1500 mm diameter; 180° = 1500 mm × 1200 mm; explicitly uses M.R. (módulo de referência) 800 × 1200 mm. SBi-anvisning 230/BR18 (DK): three-tier A/B/C quality levels; C = code minimum (BR18); B = comfort/best practice for WC users; A = care/residential level. ESKEH (FI): Invalidiliitto accessibility audit framework; pyörätuoli kääntöpaikka 1500 mm minimum; sähköpyörätuoli 2500 mm outdoor turning recommended. CEUD Building for Everyone (IE): NDA/CEUD series; Building Regulations Part M 2022 (latest includes Changing Places). NZS 4121:2001 (NZ): 1500 mm diameter manoeuvring circle; G3/AS1 acceptable solution.
references/bpc/population-general/mobility-built-environment.md:24:**Opus 4.6 synthesis note (2026-03-29):** Synthesis reviewed. This is the most evidence-rich BPC in the compendium (20+ key sources, 24 jurisdictions, Tier 1 IDeA Center anthropometric research). Five findings. (1) The 1524 mm ADA rejection is correct and well-evidenced (IDeA Center, Summer Foundation/UTS, Flemmer 2025 NZ). The guidebook’s tier-ladder (1500 code / 1700 best practice / 1800 power WC) is the most defensible specification structure across all reviewed BPCs. Cross-reference bathroom BPC Opus synthesis: the bathroom turning circle inherits this tier-ladder (1500 standard / 1800 power WC). (2) The grab bar type divergence (ADA horizontal vs evidence-based vertical/bilateral) is correctly identified as unresolved. The bathroom BPC Opus synthesis provides the resolution: Kennedy et al. 2015 (Tier 1) demonstrates vertical bars produce smallest COP deviation; bilateral provision serves both transfer directions. The guidebook should specify both horizontal AND vertical as the combined best practice, not choose one. (3) The IT three-tier framework (accessibility/visitability/adaptability) and DK three-quality-level framework (A/B/C) are structurally analogous to the guidebook’s own Universal Mode/1/2 hierarchy. This convergence should be explicitly noted in Part 1 §1.4 as international precedent. (4) The Clemson et al. 2023 Cochrane review (38% fall reduction from OT-delivered home hazard reduction) is the strongest single piece of evidence supporting the guidebook’s core premise that OT involvement in built environment design produces measurably better outcomes. This should be prominently cited in Part 1 §1.3 and Part 9 §9.2. (5) No cross-population conflict identified for MOB provisions. MOB turning circles, ramp gradients, and door widths are beneficial or neutral for all other populations. MOB is the only population code with zero conflict flags across all synthesised BPCs. Evidence confidence: HIGH (Tier 1 anthropometric data, Tier 3 Cochrane systematic reviews, 24-jurisdiction convergence on core provisions).

references/bpc/population-general/neurological-built-environment.md:25:### Best-practice synthesis
references/bpc/population-general/neurological-built-environment.md:34:**Opus 4.6 synthesis note (2026-03-29):** Synthesis reviewed. Two findings. (1) The NEU population is the most heterogeneous in the guidebook — it encompasses ABI, stroke, MS, Parkinson’s, epilepsy, and PCS. The synthesis correctly identifies navigation impairment sub-typing (egocentric/topographic/landmark agnosia) as the Tier 2 assessment framework. However, the unilateral neglect provision (high-contrast cues on neglected side) is clinically sound but architecturally challenging — buildings cannot reliably determine which side a user neglects. Resolution: bilateral redundancy (cues on both sides) is the Tier 1 provision; unilateral-specific placement is Tier 2 only (OT assessment of individual user). (2) The NEU→MOB co-occurrence is the most common in clinical practice. The bathroom BPC Opus synthesis adds NEU-specific provisions (hemiplegic vertical bars, Nakamura 2009). Wayfinding provisions (D-02, D-04, D-08) should cross-reference NEU explicitly, not only DEM. Evidence confidence: MODERATE (directional principles well-supported; quantified thresholds thin; population heterogeneity limits specification precision).
references/bpc/population-general/ot-cpg-built-environment.md:36:**Opus 4.6 synthesis note (2026-03-29):** This is a reference BPC for the Co-2 evidence tier, not a specification BPC. Opus review confirms it as the governing source list for OT clinical practice guideline evidence. One finding: the RCOT Housing Adaptations Without Delay (2019) is cited across 6+ other BPCs as the primary UK Co-2 source. The AOTA Home Modification Practice Guidelines (2023) and CAOT Home Assessment and Modifications (2024) are the US and CA equivalents. These three sources together form the Co-2 evidence spine for residential item specifications. The guidebook’s §1.5 Evidence Hierarchy should cite all three explicitly as the Co-2 exemplars. WFOT (2019) position statement on home modifications provides the international professional framework. Evidence confidence: HIGH (these are verified professional body publications with known authorship, publication dates, and institutional backing).

references/bpc/sensory-environment/room-acoustic-performance.md:20:### Best-practice synthesis
references/bpc/sensory-environment/room-acoustic-performance.md:25:Best-practice provision: RT60 ≤ 0.3 s in classrooms ≤ 283 m³. This requirement is now peer-reviewed (Iglehart, 2020, AJA) and formally encoded in ANSI/ASA S12.60-2010/Part 1 Footnote e. It applies to children with hearing aids or cochlear implants. The standard general-population requirement (0.6 s) is demonstrably insufficient for hearing device users; speech perception scores are significantly better at 0.3 s than 0.6 s for this population. Background noise target: ≤ 30–35 dB(A) (more stringent than the standard ≤ 35 dB(A)).
references/bpc/sensory-environment/room-acoustic-performance.md:28:Best-practice provision: No internationally agreed quantified RT60 target specific to autistic users. Bettarello et al. (2021, *Applied Sciences*) and Caniato et al. (2024) confirm that existing standards (ANSI/ASA S12.60, BB93, UNI 11532-2) are calibrated to neurotypical populations and are insufficient for NDV/AUT. Autistic users are significantly more affected by modest background noise increases (52→55 dB(A)) and by sudden noise events than neurotypical users. Evidence supports: lower background noise targets (≤ 35 dB(A); aspiration: ≤ 30 dB(A)), broadband absorption to suppress flutter echo and reflective peaks, no sound masking systems (A-13 doctrine), and sensory gradient zoning (F-01). Sound masking is contraindicated for NDV/AUT.
references/bpc/sensory-environment/room-acoustic-performance.md:31:Best-practice provision: Acoustic calm as primary therapeutic intervention. BrainXchange (Canada, Tier 2 Co-1) documents background noise management as clinically significant for dementia care. Devos et al. (2019, PMC) confirm RT60 measurement and acoustic intervention as standard practice in Belgian nursing homes, with measurable outcomes. Lyngby-Taarbæk case study (Part IX-06) documents 40% reduction in agitation events following acoustic ceiling installation. Targets consistent with NDV: NC-25 (≤ 35 dB(A)), RT60 ≤ 0.5 s in occupied common areas.
references/bpc/sensory-environment/room-acoustic-performance.md:34:Best-practice provision: Flicker-free, low background noise, NC-25 or better. No specific RT60 target for PCS confirmed beyond general accessibility guidance. The PCS population is absent from all room acoustic standards reviewed in any language.
references/bpc/sensory-environment/room-acoustic-performance.md:132:**Already in BPC:** Iglehart 2020 (REF-RAP-11), Murgia 2022 (REF-RAP-12), Devos 2019 (REF-RAP-13)
references/bpc/sensory-environment/room-acoustic-performance.md:225:**REF-RAP-23 (Prodi & Visentin 2022, Tier 3):** n=302 Italian children aged 11–13. Small RT increase (0.57→0.69 s) combined with classroom noise produced statistically significant listening effort increase and accuracy drop for speech perception task (grade 6 most affected). Confirms even sub-threshold RT changes have measurable consequences. Supports precision of RT targets in BPC.
references/bpc/sensory-environment/room-acoustic-performance.md:237:- No contradictions found with existing BPC specifications
references/bpc/sensory-environment/room-acoustic-performance.md:245:**Conflict:** BPC consensus finding row 6 (NRC ≥ 0.85 panels as primary treatment) vs REF-RAP-22 (Amlani & Russo 2016: panels degraded listening effort despite STI compliance).
references/bpc/sensory-environment/room-acoustic-performance.md:260:**BPC row 6 annotation:** [CONTRADICTED BY FDR: REF-RAP-22 (Amlani & Russo 2016) demonstrates NRC-compliant panels can increase listening effort beyond critical distance. NRC ≥ 0.85 necessary but insufficient; spectral balance and position-specific STI verification required.]

references/bpc/sensory-environment/school-environment-autism.md:13:### Best-practice synthesis
references/bpc/sensory-environment/school-environment-autism.md:38:bpc_path: references/bpc/sensory-environment/school-environment-autism.md
references/bpc/sensory-environment/sensory-processing-model-design-application.md:24:**Opus 4.6 synthesis note (2026-03-29):** This BPC is a framework entry, not a specification entry. Opus review confirms it as the governing theoretical framework for all F-series and sensory-related item specifications. Three findings. (1) The four-profile model (seeking/avoiding/sensitivity/low-registration) correctly identifies that no single environmental setting serves all NDV users. The Detectable Gradient Protocol (three-zone spatial model) is the primary resolution. Individual user control is the secondary resolution. These two mechanisms together provide Tier 1 and Tier 2 coverage. (2) The Allen CDM integration note is critical for DEM+NDV co-occurrence: CDM addresses progressive cognitive decline; Dunn’s model addresses static sensory variation. In facilities serving both populations (aged care with NDV residents), specifications must satisfy both frameworks simultaneously. This is a design constraint, not a conflict — CDM-simplified environments (low complexity, consistent layout) are compatible with sensory-avoiding/sensory-sensitivity provisions. The conflict arises only with sensory-seeking provisions in dementia settings, where stimulating environments may increase agitation. Route to cross-population-conflict-mapper. (3) PAS 6463:2022 is correctly identified as the sole national standard operationalising this framework. No other jurisdiction has equivalent regulation. This means all NDV sensory specifications in the guidebook exceed any mandatory requirement — they are Tier 4–5 (beyond-code best practice). Evidence confidence: HIGH for the theoretical framework (Dunn 1997 is Tier 1 OT clinical research with extensive replication); LOW for specific built-environment applications of the framework (no RCT validating specific design thresholds derived from the model).

references/bpc/sensory-environment/therapeutic-lighting-design.md:14:**Opus synthesis note:** Metric transition alert — this entry uses EML (equivalent melanopic lux) values (≥150–200 EML). The circadian-lighting-melanopic-edi BPC uses the newer melanopic EDI metric (≥250 melanopic EDI). Conversion: EML = 1.104 × melanopic EDI. Thus 200 EML ≈ 181 melanopic EDI, which is below the 250 melanopic EDI threshold in the circadian slug. The discrepancy reflects the source literature: older RCTs report EML, Brown et al. 2022 recommends in melanopic EDI. For specification purposes, use melanopic EDI ≥250 as the unified daytime threshold (per circadian slug); the ≥2500 lux photopic / ≥200 EML values are historical RCT reporting, not the recommended design target.

references/connections/cross-cutting/connections.md:172:**Source BPC slug(s):** mental-health-built-environment
references/connections/cross-cutting/connections.md:179:**Connection:** The MH BPC documents that exceeding bed capacity in psychiatric wards produces OR 5.36 for aggression (Weltens 2023, experience sampling method). This is a built-environment capacity specification: the number of beds per ward is a design parameter with a direct, large, quantified effect on safety outcomes. The OR is among the largest in the MH BPC evidence base — comparable to the absence of private space (van der Schaaf 2013).
references/connections/cross-cutting/connections.md:183:Additionally, the MH BPC identifies that ward-level environmental factors (capacity, private space, sensory modulation availability) govern coercive measure use MORE than patient-level factors or staffing. This inverts the typical clinical assumption that patient behaviour drives restraint use.
references/connections/cross-cutting/connections.md:185:**Evidence basis:** MH BPC: Weltens 2023 (ESM, OR 5.36 for aggression when capacity exceeded). van der Schaaf 2013 (n=23,868 — ward design variables > staffing variables for coercion). Husum 2010 (n=1,016 — ward-level variation in coercion not explained by patient characteristics).
references/connections/cross-cutting/connections.md:200:**Source BPC slug(s):** methodology-evidence-hierarchy-mapping (Phase 1A), mental-health-built-environment
references/connections/cross-cutting/connections.md:206:**Connection:** Phase 1A §7.4 states the ● / ○ system does not further stratify within ●. But the MH BPC contains Faerden 2022 (d=2.0), CAPABLE (RCT, hospitalisation halved), and Clemson Cochrane (38% fall reduction) — all ●, but the effect sizes differ by an order of magnitude. Part 1 should cite the d=2.0 as the upper anchor of ● evidence, demonstrating the range within the marker. This strengthens the methodology transparency commitment (Phase 1A §10.2) without changing the ● / ○ system.

references/connections/cross-domain-gap-analysis-2026-04-09.md:68:**What's missing:** Fire doors held closed (fire code requirement) break spatial continuity for DEM users (Marquardt 2011: floor plan is the most influential environmental factor for orientation) and sightlines for DEAF users (DeafSpace: visual connectivity for signing and environmental awareness). No item code, BPC, or connection addresses this conflict.

Environment must reduce propulsion effort. Existing connections cover ramp gradient and door force. But propulsion-reduction is BUILDING-WIDE: A-09 corridor surface friction (carpet vs hard — rolling resistance), A-02 corridor distance (shorter routes reduce cumulative shoulder load), A-07 cross-slope (any deviation increases unilateral shoulder load), E-07 threshold transitions (each bump is bilateral force spike). Currently specified for wheelchair ACCESS not INJURY PREVENTION. The specification framing changes: A-02 minimum corridor width is not 'can a wheelchair fit?' but 'does the corridor minimise propulsion effort over repeated daily use?' MOB BPC explicitly flagged Sawatzky as 'Not yet mined — deferred citation-miner.'

references/connections/frameworks-and-methodology/connections.md:743:**Connection:** Clemson et al. 2023 Cochrane: OT-delivered home hazard reduction achieves 38% fall reduction (high-risk); NON-OT-delivered: non-significant effect. Gillespie et al. Cochrane (cited in Keall 2015): same finding for broader falls prevention. MOB BPC: 'OT-delivered home safety assessment more effective than non-OT delivery.' Directly supports Part 9 specification that OT assessment should PRECEDE home modification, not follow it.

references/connections/health-and-symptom-management/connections.md:99:**Connection:** Rest provision scales through three tiers — seated rest (I-03, every 50m on primary routes), enclosed low-stimulation space (D-05, one per floor), full sensory room (A-16, one per building) — but the scaling relationship is not specified. A practitioner does not know: (a) at what building occupancy does each tier become mandatory? (b) what is the distance/time threshold between tiers? (c) can D-05 substitute for A-16 in smaller buildings? These three items are specified independently. The scaling hierarchy is implicit in the BPC evidence (PAS 6463 recommends quiet spaces at building scale; OFS BPC specifies rest points at 50m intervals) but never codified.

references/connections/health-and-symptom-management/connections.md:212:**Connection:** 3.9°C gap between OFS/MS maximum (≤21°C — Strassheim 2018, CDC ME/CFS, Chaseling 2022) and DEM/older adult thermal neutral (24.9°C — thermal-comfort-older-adults BPC). Resolution synthesized in thermoregulation BPC: ambient default 18-20°C in shared spaces where NEU/MS or SCI present; individual local warmth for DEM/older adults via heated seating pad (≤45°C surface, timer-controlled), radiant panel — no ambient temperature increase. This is the second thermal conflict after MS-vs-FMS (ms-thermal BPC).

references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-2026-04-09.md:40:**Source BPC slug(s):** intellectual-disability-built-environment-design, dementia-built-environment
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-2026-04-09.md:58:The IntD "zone-differentiated ceiling heights" specification is unique — it does not appear in any other population's BPC. This should be evaluated for DEM applicability (spatial differentiation aids cognitive mapping). Conversely, DEM's "3D landmark objects at decision points" is absent from IntD but functionally relevant (reduces cognitive load at route choices).
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-2026-04-09.md:60:**Evidence basis:** IntD BPC: all findings AU (NDIS SDA) and CA (CSA B651) derived, Tier 4-5. DEM BPC: Marquardt 2011 (Tier 3), DSDC (Tier 5), 10+ jurisdictions. IntD evidence base is thinner but the convergence pattern suggests DEM evidence can be applied by analogy to IntD.
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-2026-04-09.md:73:**Source BPC slug(s):** upper-limb-impairment-built-environment, deafblind-built-environment-design
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-2026-04-09.md:80:**Connection:** UPL BPC documents that optimal grab bar grasp location varies with body height (r=0.67, Levine 2025) — fixed placement cannot serve all users. CON-0120 (this session) proposes grab bars as haptic spatial landmarks for DBL. These two findings interact: if grab bar height is variable (UPL Tier 2 provision), then DBL users cannot rely on consistent haptic landmarks for spatial orientation.
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-2026-04-09.md:88:**Evidence basis:** UPL BPC: Levine 2025 (grasp location varies with height, r=0.67). Kennedy 2015: vertical bars produce smallest COP deviation. DBL BPC: consistent tactile layout is highest priority (DbI). CON-0120: grab bar as haptic landmark.
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-2026-04-09.md:101:**Source BPC slug(s):** neurological-built-environment, visual-impairment-built-environment
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-2026-04-09.md:108:**Connection:** NEU BPC Opus synthesis establishes bilateral redundancy as the Tier 1 provision for hemispatial neglect: environmental cues on BOTH sides of corridors, because unilateral neglect makes one side invisible. VIS BPC specifies signage at eye level on both sides of corridors for legibility from either approach direction. Both populations independently require bilateral environmental cues — NEU for neglect compensation, VIS for approach-direction legibility.
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-2026-04-09.md:114:**Evidence basis:** NEU BPC Opus synthesis: bilateral redundancy is Tier 1 for unilateral neglect. VIS BPC: signage on both sides is standard practice (BS 8300, ISO 21542). The convergence is mechanistically different (NEU = compensating for perceptual deletion; VIS = compensating for approach uncertainty) but specificationally identical.
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-2026-04-09.md:127:**Source BPC slug(s):** ofs-built-environment, visual-impairment-built-environment
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-2026-04-09.md:134:**Connection:** OFS BPC specifies rest seating every 25-30m on primary routes (tightened from BS 8300's 50m for MOB). VIS BPC specifies continuous TWSI on primary routes with attention indicators at decision points (ISO 23599). These specifications occupy the same physical space — the primary circulation route — but are specified independently.
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-2026-04-09.md:140:**Evidence basis:** OFS BPC: 25-30m rest intervals. VIS BPC: ISO 23599 attention indicators at decision points + facilities. The coordination is logical inference — no study validates the dual function, but the mechanism (cane-detectable furniture as landmark) is established in VIS wayfinding literature.
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-2026-04-09.md:153:**Source BPC slug(s):** deaf-spatial-design, sensory-processing-model-design-application, dementia-built-environment
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-2026-04-09.md:164:- **DEM:** Colour-coded zones for spatial wayfinding — different colours per functional area (DEM BPC, DSDC). Requires colour VARIATION between zones.
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-2026-04-09.md:170:**Evidence basis:** deaf-spatial-design BPC: muted greens/blues, no busy patterns, skin tone contrast. sensory-processing-model BPC: visual noise reduction. dementia-built-environment BPC: colour-coded wayfinding. No source addresses the three-way interaction.
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-2026-04-09.md:183:**Source BPC slug(s):** deafblind-built-environment-design, mobility-built-environment
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-2026-04-09.md:190:**Connection:** MOB BPC specifies 1800mm turning circle in bathrooms. DBL BPC specifies intervenor clear floor space ≥900×1500mm at service counters (GAP-NEW-01). In a residential bathroom, a DBL user with an intervenor needs BOTH MOB turning space AND intervenor standing space simultaneously — the intervenor stands alongside the DBL user during transfers and orientation.
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-2026-04-09.md:194:No existing standard specifies the combined spatial requirement. The DBL BPC notes GAP-NEW-01 (intervenor space at service counters) but does not extend this to residential bathrooms — arguably the highest-risk environment for DBL users.
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-2026-04-09.md:196:**Evidence basis:** DBL BPC: intervenor clear floor space ≥900×1500mm (DbI guidelines). MOB BPC: 1800mm turning (IDeA Center). Additive spatial requirement is geometric — no study needed to confirm that two bodies occupy more space than one.
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-2026-04-09.md:209:**Source BPC slug(s):** pain-ofs-built-environment-design, intellectual-disability-built-environment-design
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-2026-04-09.md:216:**Connection:** PAIN BPC specifies storage at 750-1050mm throughout — the zone between hip and shoulder that avoids bending or overhead reaching. IntD BPC does not specify storage height, but IntD users benefit from predictable, visible, consistent storage heights — not because of physical limitation but because finding items in unpredictable locations increases cognitive load and triggers frustration/distress.
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-2026-04-09.md:222:**Evidence basis:** PAIN/OFS BPC: storage 750-1050mm (energy conservation). IntD BPC: no storage guidance but "consistent predictable layout" is the highest-priority principle. DEM BPC: visual accessibility for items in daily use.
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-2026-04-09.md:235:**Source BPC slug(s):** dementia-built-environment, intellectual-disability-built-environment-design, ofs-built-environment
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-2026-04-09.md:242:**Connection:** DEM BPC specifies toilet visible from primary occupied space (CON-0018, Marquardt 2011 — reduces incontinence). IntD BPC specifies reception/assistance point within sight of entrance (CSA B651 §4.7). OFS BPC specifies rest seating within 25-30m of any point.
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-2026-04-09.md:250:**Evidence basis:** DEM BPC: Marquardt 2011 (toilet visibility strongest environmental factor). IntD BPC: CSA B651 §4.7 (reception within sight of entrance). OFS BPC: rest provision intervals. CON-0018: toilet sightline for DEM. CON-0068: toilet visibility for DEM/NEU/NDV/OFS.

references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-batch3-2026-04-09.md:183:**Source BPC slug(s):** mental-health-built-environment
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-batch3-2026-04-09.md:190:**Connection:** The MH BPC documents that exceeding bed capacity in psychiatric wards produces OR 5.36 for aggression (Weltens 2023, experience sampling method). This is a built-environment capacity specification: the number of beds per ward is a design parameter with a direct, large, quantified effect on safety outcomes. The OR is among the largest in the MH BPC evidence base — comparable to the absence of private space (van der Schaaf 2013).
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-batch3-2026-04-09.md:194:Additionally, the MH BPC identifies that ward-level environmental factors (capacity, private space, sensory modulation availability) govern coercive measure use MORE than patient-level factors or staffing. This inverts the typical clinical assumption that patient behaviour drives restraint use.
references/connections/opus-bpc-crossref-scan-batch3-2026-04-09.md:196:**Evidence basis:** MH BPC: Weltens 2023 (ESM, OR 5.36 for aggression when capacity exceeded). van der Schaaf 2013 (n=23,868 — ward design variables > staffing variables for coercion). references/connections/opus-context-synthesis-batch4-2026-04-09.md:85:**Connection:** MOB BPC: ADA 1524mm turning circle rejected; 1800mm best practice; CSA B651 2100mm for 95th-percentile power chairs. DEM BPC: toilet visible from bedroom doorway; loop circulation; no dead-ends. In residential care where MOB+DEM co-occur (the most common co-occurrence in aged care), the turning circle and the toilet-sightline specifications interact: a 1800mm turning circle placed in a bathroom may block the toilet-sightline from the bedroom door if the door swing and turning space are not coordinated. The spatial layout must simultaneously satisfy: DEM sightline (visual axis from bedroom door to toilet), MOB turning (1800mm inscribed circle), and door swing (clear opening 900mm without intruding into turning space).

references/connections/opus-context-synthesis-batch4-2026-04-09.md:132:**Source BPC slug(s):** visual-impairment-built-environment, deaf-spatial-design, deafblind-built-environment-design
references/connections/opus-context-synthesis-batch4-2026-04-09.md:135:**Evidence tier:** Co-1 (DeafSpace) + Tier 4-6 (VIS BPC)
references/connections/opus-context-synthesis-batch4-2026-04-09.md:137:**Connection:** DEAF BPC: ≥300 lux diffuse, matte-reflected, shadow-free lighting in communication zones; backlighting eliminated; lighting serves sign language visibility. VIS BPC: ≥300 lux in circulation without glare; no sudden illuminance transitions >5:1. These targets are identical in value (≥300 lux) and complementary in character (both require diffuse, glare-free light). But the rationale is different: DEAF needs light on the signer's face and hands; VIS needs light on environmental surfaces for legibility.
references/connections/opus-context-synthesis-batch4-2026-04-09.md:152:**Source BPC slug(s):** intellectual-disability-built-environment-design, pain-ofs-built-environment-design
references/connections/opus-context-synthesis-batch4-2026-04-09.md:156:**Connection:** IntD BPC: "reception/assistance point within sight of entrance" (CSA B651 §4.7). OFS BPC: "rest seating within 25–30m." In a healthcare or education building serving both populations, the entrance sequence must provide BOTH: visible assistance AND immediate rest. These are complementary, not competing: a reception desk with adjacent seated waiting serves both requirements simultaneously. But no specification links them.
references/connections/opus-economics-batch7-2026-04-09.md:14:**Source BPC slug(s):** accessible-design-economics-cost-premium, government-grant-programmes-home-adaptation
references/connections/opus-economics-batch7-2026-04-09.md:21:**Connection:** All government adaptation programmes fund retrofit exclusively — no programme funds design-stage construction. UK DFG spends £711m/year on retrofits averaging £12,000–15,000/dwelling. If those dwellings had been built accessibly, the cost would have been ~£2,000–4,000/dwelling (1% of median build cost). The grant budget would fund 3–7× more accessible homes if spent at construction. This policy misallocation is the strongest policy argument in the guidebook but is not calculated in any BPC.
references/connections/opus-economics-batch7-2026-04-09.md:23:**Evidence basis:** Economics BPC (0.94–3.92% new-build). Grant BPC (£711m/year DFG). KfW/Prognos (€19,100/dwelling retrofit, 700,000+ dwellings). Visitability ($100–600).

references/connections/opus-underscanned-bpc-batch5-2026-04-09.md:14:**Source BPC slug(s):** wayfinding-cognitive-science-spatial-design, detectable-gradient-protocol-sensory-zones
references/connections/opus-underscanned-bpc-batch5-2026-04-09.md:21:**Connection:** The cognitive-science BPC establishes "≤2 decision points visible simultaneously" as a cognitive load specification. The detectable-gradient-protocol specifies multi-sensory zone boundaries (LRV change, RT60 change, luminance change) at every transition. Zone boundary signals occurring at a wayfinding decision point ADD to information load — creating the maximum cognitive load condition (simultaneous navigation decision + sensory transition). For DEM/NEU/ABI: exceeds degraded executive function. For NDV/AUT: sensory overload at the moment requiring focused attention. For VIS: contrast changes at junctions may mask directional cues.
references/connections/opus-underscanned-bpc-batch5-2026-04-09.md:23:**Evidence basis:** Sweller 1988 (extraneous cognitive load reduces available processing capacity); O'Neill 1991 (spatial configuration outperforms signage); detectable-gradient-protocol BPC (multi-sensory redundancy at transitions). The interaction is a direct application of cognitive load theory — never stated in either BPC.

A-16 (sensory retreat) and biophilic breakout serve COMPLEMENTARY functions for DIFFERENT NDV subtypes in the SAME building.

references/connections/wayfinding-and-signage/connections.md:788:**Connection:** NEU BPC Opus synthesis establishes bilateral redundancy as the Tier 1 provision for hemispatial neglect: environmental cues on BOTH sides of corridors, because unilateral neglect makes one side invisible. VIS BPC specifies signage at eye level on both sides of corridors for legibility from either approach direction. Both populations independently require bilateral environmental cues — NEU for neglect compensation, VIS for approach-direction legibility.
references/connections/wayfinding-and-signage/connections.md:794:**Evidence basis:** NEU BPC Opus synthesis: bilateral redundancy is Tier 1 for unilateral neglect. The convergence is mechanistically different (NEU = compensating for perceptual deletion; VIS = compensating for approach uncertainty) but specificationally identical.

references/connections/wayfinding-and-signage/connections.md:842:**Connection:** The `luminance-contrast-lrv-evidence-base` BPC documents that the universal 30% LRV threshold has no empirical basis — it is a regulatory floor adopted from UK DDA guidance without validation. Severe VI needs ≥65% Michelson contrast (2.5× the standard). The guidebook recommends ≥50% LRV as best practice for C-items.
references/connections/wayfinding-and-signage/connections.md:844:The inconsistency: the `detectable-gradient-protocol-sensory-zones` BPC specifies ≥30 LRV change at zone boundaries — inheriting the unvalidated threshold. Cognitive wayfinding items depend on contrast-based landmarks for DEM, IntD, NDV. The guidebook's own ≥50% best-practice target is not propagated to zone boundaries or wayfinding items.
references/connections/wayfinding-and-signage/connections.md:854:**Action required:** Apply ≥50% LRV best-practice target consistently to all contrast-dependent provisions — C-items, zone boundaries, wayfinding items. At critical junctions (platform edges, stair nosings, kerb lines): ≥65% Michelson. The 30% value remains as code-compliance minimum only. Internal consistency correction — the guidebook already established the right position in the LRV BPC.

references/connections/wayfinding-and-signage/connections.md:926:**Connection:** FDR-CMP-04 compound interaction: DEM + VIS dual loss makes both tactile wayfinding (designed for VIS) and colour-coded wayfinding (designed for DEM) simultaneously inaccessible. BPC wayfinding-dementia confirms that DEM residents navigate via sequential decisions and landmarks, not cognitive maps. When VIS is added, landmark visibility fails. The only design solution that works for the compound case is sequential-decision-point architecture — physical layout that eliminates the need for either cognitive mapping or visual scanning. This principle also serves IntD (simplified decision nodes). MODERATE confidence: theoretical derivation from two verified evidence bases, not directly tested in a compound population study.
references/connections/wayfinding-and-signage/connections.md:928:**Evidence basis:** BPC wayfinding-dementia consensus (van Buuren 2025 PMC11931140); Marquardt 2011 (T1 verified); ISO 21542:2021 §9 multi-sensory redundancy.

references/connections/wayfinding-and-signage/connections.md:1018:**Connection:** Marquardt & Schmieg 2009 finding — floor plan configuration is the most influential environmental factor for wayfinding; signage/colour alone cannot compensate for poor layout — is cited in DEM and NEU BPCs but not IntD. IntD BPC independently specifies loop/radial circulation and no blind corners but without citing Marquardt or articulating the 'layout > signage' hierarchy. IntD wayfinding difficulty (limited spatial abstraction, difficulty interpreting novel signage) means IntD users are EQUALLY dependent on layout legibility over signage quality. The Marquardt principle transfers directly: for all populations with cognitive wayfinding impairment, layout specification must PRECEDE signage specification in the design process.

references/fdr/fold-down-grab-bar-specification.md:50:**Clinical reasoning:** For unilateral UPL the design problem is laterality-dependent in a way it is not for bilateral users. The fold-down bar position must be specified relative to the user's functional side, not as a population-average bilateral provision. This is the OT reasoning: assess which side is functional → specify bar on that side. For a bilateral household, a fold-down on each side (one deployed for the current user, both available for future occupants) is the DAR best practice.

references/methodology/value-genealogy-worked-example-corridor-width.md:28:Consequence for adjudication: **values are commensurable only within a measurement paradigm.** A 1500mm static turning circle cannot corroborate *or* contradict a 2400mm enclosed-bay swept envelope — they measure different physical events. The genealogy schema therefore records `measurement_paradigm` per extracted value, and the independence count runs *within* paradigm. The corpus has already deprecated "turning circle/radius" as a synthesis parameter in favour of "manoeuvring footprint / swept envelope qualified by manoeuvre type + drive system" (methodology BPC §5).

references/project-standards.md:8:RULE: THE PURPOSE OF THIS GUIDEBOOK IS TO GET PEOPLE TO ASK THE RIGHT QUESTIONS. This is the most important principle governing the entire project. The guidebook is not a prescription manual. It is not an authority on measurements. It does not dictate values that designers, policymakers, or practitioners must apply. It is a thinking tool that equips people to ask the right questions about how to design for accessibility depending on the circumstance. Measurements, ranges, and reference data exist to support this process — they serve the questions, not the other way around. Every item specification, every BPC synthesis, every piece of guidebook prose must be evaluated against this standard: does it help the reader ask better questions about this design element? Does it surface considerations they would not have encountered otherwise? Does it make them think more critically about the specific situation they face? When you know better, you do better. A designer who knows what questions to ask will produce a better outcome than one who does not — even without perfection, even without specialist input. The guidebook aims to raise the floor of understanding for everyone who touches the built environment.
references/project-standards.md:17:RULE: Evidence hierarchy is seven tiers, per governance/tier-system.md (OPERATIVE 2026-05-25, owner directive "t2>t3 this is enshrined"; DR-2026-05-29 ACCEPTED 2026-07-13). Tier 1 = primary research with intervention-level or biomechanical control (OT-prioritized, not OT-exclusive, per D-E); Co-1 = lived experience / participatory design (CRPD Art. 4.3, co-primary with Tier 1); Tier 2 = synthesis — (a) systematic reviews / meta-analyses AND (b) named-organisation evidence-based standards; Co-2 = OT professional body CPGs (co-primary with Tier 2); Tier 3 = lower-control primary clinical research + grey-literature primary research (supporting; rarely the sole basis — T3-alone never reaches `stated`, per the tier3-stated-threshold DR); Tiers 4–6 = the regulatory stratum (international standards, national frameworks, statutory codes) — walled off from best-practice anchoring; convergence-not-evidence. The evidence hierarchy determines what constitutes best practice. Where higher-tier evidence exists, it governs.
references/project-standards.md:20:RULE: Best practice means the most accommodating, thoughtful, respectful, dignified, and usable condition achievable for the disabled person. Best practice is determined by the evidence hierarchy — Tier 1 primary research, Co-1 lived experience, Tier 2 synthesis (SR/MA + named-organisation evidence-based standards), Co-2 OT CPGs — not by code consensus. Codes are Tier 6: the compliance floor, not the aspiration. Code consensus across jurisdictions establishes what most codes agree on; it does not establish what is most accommodating or most dignified. A BPC best_practice_synthesis that derives its value solely from code consensus is a weak-band (○) best-practice claim — "best practice as currently known," valid only when flagged code-derived with the convergence-not-evidence caveat, and never rendered unflagged or above the weak band (amended 2026-07-21, owner directive, Option A; `decisions/DR-2026-07-21-evidence-architecture-option-a-execution.md`). An unflagged or full-strength code-consensus best-practice claim is in error. The test: does this specification provide the most accommodating, dignified, usable condition the evidence supports — or does it merely reflect what codes agree on?

references/project-standards.md:172:RULE: Specification language is tier-appropriate and does not claim authority the project does not have. The guidebook is an advocacy project (see Core Doctrine), not a standard-setting body. Specification constructions by mode: Universal Mode — "Code requires [value] per [standard]" (authority is the code, not the guidebook). Population Mode — "[Evidence tier] evidence supports [value]" or "Best practice based on [N] jurisdictions and [tier] evidence is [value]" (authority is the evidence). Person Mode — "OT assessment determines position within [range] based on [functional parameter]" (authority is the OT). The former convention of blanket "shall be" constructions is retired — "shall be" implies mandating authority the project does not possess. Always run prose-style-checker before vol2-item-formatter. Existing Part 4 text using "shall be" requires a voice pass (A4 or C-stage find-and-replace).

references/project-standards.md:582:RULE: Merge implies ratification. When the owner merges a branch/PR to `main`, that act ratifies every decision, Decision Record, governance proposal, and rule-change the merge contains — with the same force as an explicit "ratify" directive — UNLESS the owner explicitly notes otherwise on that merge (e.g. "merging to iterate, not ratified", "staged only"). This ends the standing ambiguity where PROPOSED artifacts sat merged-but-formally-unratified, risking owner-directed work being treated as never-authorized and left unimplemented. Scope and limits: (1) merge ratifies the DECISION; it does not by itself COMPLETE staged/deferred EXECUTION a DR gates behind ratification — those items become authorized-and-owed, tracked in the ratification-execution register, not silently done. (2) It does not waive genuine external preconditions a DR names (e.g. an owner-only input like the deployed `<audit_trail>` list, or a doctrine-SHA-cascade edit requiring the materiality triage) — those remain real work, now authorized. (3) It does not convert an evidence-maturity `provisional`/`pending` cell or BPC to `stated`; evidence state is governed by evidence strength, not ratification. (4) DG-NON items still require the owner's substantive direction to have occurred — merge ratifies what the owner decided, it does not manufacture a decision the owner never made. On merge, flip stale PROPOSED/PENDING status text on the merged artifacts to ratified-by-merge (dated), and reconcile the execution register so nothing authorized is left tracked as un-authorized.
references/project-standards.md:606:RULE: Model routing names a CLASS, never a version. All model-routing text — decision records, skill headers, workplan phase tables, governance prose — names a model class (`opus`, `fable`, `sonnet`, `haiku`, `human`) and never a version number. Version numbers are stripped on touch. Rationale: a version pin dates the moment it is written, and a rule pinned to a retired number reads as excluding the model that replaced it — which is how a routing FLOOR silently becomes a routing CEILING. This restates and completes DR-2026-06-10-synthesis-model-floor, which ratified rule #2 as a capability floor ("Opus-class or above") and whose §4 owed a caller sweep it did not perform. references/project-standards.md:642:RULE: Adversarial review is a truth-instrument bound to evidence, never a plan-instrument. An adversarial pass may be commissioned ONLY against a diff that (a) wrote rows to the research tables (`search_executions`, `search_candidates`, `evidence_sources`, `source_slug_links`, `evidence_population_match`, `source_value_extractions`, `specifications`, `convergence_assessment`, `jurisdictional_values`, `case_studies`, `economics_entries`) or (b) authored or amended a synthesis artifact (`references/bpc-reasoning/*`, `best_practice_synthesis`, a rendered determination page). Plans, critiques, censuses, handoffs, registers, session records, Decision Records and this ledger are not adversarial-pass subjects; they receive the mechanical gates already registered and nothing more. The rule was earned by measurement: **at least ten fresh-context adversarial passes ran between 2026-07-14 and 2026-08-19, and not one examined research output**, because there is none — every research table stands at zero rows. The fresh-session independence convention (`workplan/2026-08-15-adversarial-brief-pr103.md` §0, "Run this in fresh context. Do not read the authoring session's reasoning first") is epistemically correct AND is the mechanism guaranteeing a new session per critique, so critique → plan → critique became the tightest loop in the repository. The one counter-example is the standard to copy: `sessions/session_2026-07-26-energy-conservation-rest-points-seating-adversarial.md`, the only pass ever run on research output, produced **seven sustained findings in a single session**, all against the author's own admitted batch, catching error in both directions — a T1-candidate under-tiered at T3 and a no-participants discussion piece over-tiered, plus one dataset admitted twice under two ref_ids and a circular value. Its own diagnosis is the thing this rule protects: *"a claim pitched at a confidence the retrieval didn't earn."* **The agonist needs no construction: R1-R15 already compel the authoring session to file its complete affirmative case as rows.** The antagonist attacks that recorded case through named lenses — existence, fidelity, independence, tier, population, contrary-finding, recognition by the population served, and query-shape — and the cheapest agonist-antagonist mechanic is blind-then-compare: re-grade tier and population-match independently BEFORE seeing the author's grades, then diff. A pass whose subject is a plan cannot be wrong about anything a reader could check.

workplan/2026-10-30-ramp-spec-pages/owner-rules/spec-page-requirements.md:35:**DEFINITION OF BEST PRACTICE (owner, 2026-10-29, stated repeatedly; supersedes any "Guidebook position/working position"):** the Guidebook takes no positions. Best practice = the best way to do something according to how it benefits the intended group; it is NOT the most common or most agreed value. It is the most accommodating/gentlest value found in any current standard (including preferred values) unless an academic article or professional body improves on it. Never present "most common" or "agreed" values as best practice; never label something a Guidebook position or recommendation. Judge per item and per population: the question is always who benefits and how much. Legal maximums are floors for comparison, shown as such.

workplan/best-practices-assessment-system.md:1:# Best-Practices Assessment System — Design
workplan/best-practices-assessment-system.md:5:**Core gap it closes:** the mission defines a per-cell best-practice determination, but `specifications` is **empty (0 rows)** — the determination engine is unbuilt.
workplan/best-practices-assessment-system.md:11:Your mission already prescribes *how* best practice is decided. "Best practice is determined by the evidence hierarchy, not code consensus" (doctrine #2), and every `(parameter × population)` cell must carry one of four states (doctrine #4): **`stated`** (≥Tier 3 OR Co‑1 OR Co‑2), **`provisional`**, **`pending`**, **`not_applicable`**. The system's job is to *apply* this consistently, dynamically, and auditably across all cells. It must never let a code-only determination render above **weak-band (○), flagged, "best practice as currently known"** — a Tier‑6-only cell stays `provisional`, never `stated`, and code is the floor (amended 2026-07-21, Option A; `decisions/DR-2026-07-21-evidence-architecture-option-a-execution.md`).
workplan/best-practices-assessment-system.md:38:   - `pending` ⟺ sparse across all dimensions → emit `[BEST-PRACTICE-PENDING]` + link to a `gaps` row.
workplan/best-practices-assessment-system.md:45:6. **Falsification condition:** every `stated`/`provisional` cell records *what evidence would overturn it* (defends against the known BPC‑hallucination failure mode; ties to `gaps.falsification_condition`).
workplan/best-practices-assessment-system.md:53:**SUPERSEDED (2026-07-13):** the sketch below is superseded by the actual migration, per `decisions/DR-2026-07-12-evidence-cell-state-schema-reconciliation.md`'s own "Consequences if ratified" section: *"`workplan/best-practices-assessment-system.md` §4's SQL sketch is superseded by the actual migration; its phasing plan (§8) is otherwise unaffected."* The live schema (`scripts/migrations/026_reconcile_specifications.sql`, `027_regulatory_stratum_only.sql`) keeps `specifications`'s identity as `(item_code, population_code)` — not `(slug, population, jurisdiction)` as sketched below — and structures the within-population range as `value_min`/`value_max`/`value_unit` rather than a free-text `value_range`. Jurisdiction-specific values live in the separate `jurisdictional_values` table, deliberately not folded into this one (conflating a jurisdiction-agnostic best-practice determination with a jurisdiction-specific code floor is exactly the failure mode this schema exists to prevent — see `governance/tier-system.md` §3). The sketch is left below for the phasing-plan context (§8, unaffected); do not implement against it — implement against the live migrations.

workplan/next-steps-synthesis-2026-07-14.md:56:All four strategies keep the **same act** on the critical path: *a single, measurably-unreliable operator authoring adjudicated "best-practice" determinations.* They differ only in **volume** (S1: 82; S4: ~10), **sequence** (S3: build the jig first), or **wrapper** (S2: mail a review afterward). None removes the biased synthesis step from the critical path; none adds a standing second author; and all four quietly define review success as *gating-on-attempt*, where a logged non-response clears the gate — i.e. **they have already pre-conceded no second human will engage** (0 of 6 outreach batches sent since 2026-05-02; CI deleted 2026-06-09).
workplan/next-steps-synthesis-2026-07-14.md:66:**S5 — SHIP THE EVIDENCE MAP, NOT THE AUTHORITY.** Publish what already exists and is solo-sound: the 640-source, tier-graded, Co-1/Co-2-classified corpus as a navigable annotated index by item × population × jurisdiction, **surfacing where sources disagree** and declining to emit a single adjudicated "best-practice value." The reader performs the last-mile synthesis. This *subtracts* the adjudication layer where the 67% bias lives (the opposite move from S1–S4); it matches the mission's own language; it converts "permanently solo" from fatal to fine (indexing/grading is what solo+AI has already done to quality); the empty `conflicts` table stops being a blocker because **the disagreement becomes the product**; and it ships in weeks at a fraction of the cost. Honest boundary: tier-assignment is still a judgment, so S5 shrinks the risk surface rather than eliminating it — but it is a far smaller, more checkable surface than per-cell synthesis.
